questions.q: Two delivery datasets both average 50 minutes, but one has a standard deviation of 1.41 and the other 21.21. What does this tell you?
options: The second dataset has a lower center
The second dataset's delivery times vary far more around the same average
The first dataset has more rows
The averages must actually be different
questions.explain: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean, so a larger value means values are more spread out.

questions.q: Which measure of spread is most robust to outliers?
questions.explain: The IQR uses only the middle half of the data, so extreme values barely affect it.

questions.q: What does np.var([1, 2, 3, 4]) return by default, compared with pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4]).var()?
questions.explain: numpy defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n) while pandas defaults to ddof=1 (divide by n-1).

questions.q: Why do we divide by n minus 1 when estimating a population variance from a sample?
options: To make the number bigger for aesthetic reasons
Because a sample's values sit closer to the sample mean than to the true mean, so dividing by n underestimates the variance
Because one data point is always wasted
questions.explain: The n-1 (Bessel's) correction removes that systematic underestimate; a simulation showed about 80 with n versus about 100 with n-1.

questions.q: You have highly skewed income data and are reporting the median. Which spread measure is the natural companion?
questions.explain: Median plus IQR is the robust pairing for skewed data; mean plus standard deviation suits roughly symmetric data.
